title: The Qur'an in Islamic Civilization and in America
bigQuestion: How did one Arabic book shape languages, art, science and law across half the world, and how did it reach America?

story.title: A Life Story That Begins with a Surah
story.kicker: In 1831, an enslaved man in North Carolina picked up a pen and began his life story with the words of Surah 67.
paragraphs: In 1831, a man of about sixty sat down in North Carolina to write the story of his life. He wrote in Arabic, from right to left, in a clear and practiced hand. His name was Omar ibn Said. He had been born around 1770 in Futa Toro, a region along the Senegal River in West Africa, where he studied the Qur'an for many years.

In 1807 he was captured, marched to the coast and shipped across the Atlantic to Charleston, South Carolina. He was sold. He escaped from a harsh owner and was jailed in Fayetteville, North Carolina. There, tradition says, he wrote on the walls of his cell in Arabic with charcoal. No one in the town could read it. He was sold again, to a family named Owen, and lived with them until his death in 1864.

His life story is fifteen pages long. It does not begin with "I was born." It begins with Surah 67, Al-Mulk, "The Kingdom," written out from memory. The surah says that all dominion belongs to God, who created death and life to test which people act best. Only after the surah does Omar write about himself: his teachers, his capture, his years in America.

Scholars have asked why he opened this way. Some read it as a quiet statement to his owners: the true king is not you. Others see a man reaching for the words he knew best. Omar himself does not explain. He was one of thousands of Muslims brought to the Americas in chains, and one of very few whose own words survive.

In 2017 the Library of Congress acquired his manuscript, and in 2019 it put the pages online for anyone to read. This chapter follows the Qur'an out of Arabia: into new languages, into art and science, into law and schools, and finally, in the hand of Omar ibn Said, into America.
story.think: Why might a person open his own life story with a chapter of scripture? What would it say to readers who could read Arabic, and what to those who could not?

lessons.title: A Language Travels with a Book
lessons.mainIdea: Because Muslims recite the Qur'an in Arabic, the Arabic language and alphabet spread with Islam far beyond Arabia.
reading: Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed in Arabic, and the book says so of itself. Surah 12, Yusuf, ayah 2, says it was sent down as an Arabic Qur'an so that people might understand. For this reason, Muslims recite it in Arabic wherever they live. A child in Indonesia, Nigeria or Chicago learns the sounds of Arabic before learning what the words mean.

Within a century of Muhammad's death in 632, Muslim rule stretched from Spain to Central Asia. In many of those lands, Arabic became the language of government, learning and daily life. Iraq, Syria, Egypt and North Africa are examples. In others, such as Persia, people kept their own language. But they took in thousands of Arabic words and, above all, the Arabic alphabet.

That alphabet was the Qur'an's alphabet, and it traveled far. Persian and Ottoman Turkish were written in Arabic letters. So were Urdu in South Asia, Swahili on the East African coast and Malay in Southeast Asia. Some still are. When Omar ibn Said wrote in North Carolina, he used the same letters. A scribe in Baghdad had used them a thousand years before.

words.d: the language of the Qur'an; Muslims recite the book in Arabic wherever they live
a set of letters; the Arabic alphabet was adopted to write Persian, Turkish, Urdu, Swahili and Malay

look.title: An Arabic Qur'an
look.text: Near its opening, Surah Yusuf says that God sent it down as a lecture, or reading, in Arabic, so that its hearers may understand.
look.cite: Qur'an 12:2, Surah Yusuf, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: This verse is one reason Muslims keep the Qur'an in Arabic. What is gained by keeping one language, and what problem does it create for readers who do not know Arabic?

check.q: Why do Muslims around the world recite the Qur'an in Arabic?
choices: Because Arabic is easy to learn
Because Muslims believe it was revealed in Arabic and the book says so
Because the caliphs banned other languages
check.why: Surah 12:2 and other verses describe the Qur'an as Arabic, and Muslims keep it in that language for recitation.

check.q: Which of these languages was written in the Arabic alphabet for centuries?
check.why: Swahili, along with Persian, Ottoman Turkish, Urdu and Malay, was written in Arabic letters, some still are.

check.q: What happened to the Persian language after the arrival of Islam?
choices: It kept its own words but adopted the Arabic alphabet and many Arabic words
check.why: Persians kept their language but borrowed heavily from Arabic and wrote Persian in Arabic script.

lessons.title: Calligraphy and Pattern
lessons.mainIdea: Because writing the Qur'an beautifully became a sacred art, calligraphy and geometric pattern became the main visual arts of the Muslim world.
reading: Walk into almost any historic mosque and you will see words on the walls: verses of the Qur'an in flowing or angular letters. Most Muslim artists, following hadith that warn against images, avoided pictures of God, prophets and, in religious buildings, living beings. Writing took the place that painting holds in a church. To write the Qur'an well became the highest visual art.

The earliest Qur'ans were written in *Kufic*, a bold, angular script, often on parchment in wide pages. One famous example, the Blue Qur'an, was written in gold on parchment dyed blue in North Africa around the tenth century. In Baghdad, the scribe Ibn Muqla (d. 940) worked out rules of proportion for a rounder script. His system led to the *naskh* script, in which most Qur'ans are printed today.

Beside the letters came pattern. Artists filled walls, tiles, carpets and book pages with interlocking stars, polygons and vines. Muslim writers often said the endless repeating patterns reflect the idea of one God whose creation has order without end. Whether or not one accepts that reading, the patterns spread from Spain to India and are still made today.

words.d: the art of beautiful writing; the main religious art of the Muslim world
an early angular Arabic script used for the oldest Qur'ans
a rounded, clear Arabic script; most printed Qur'ans use it (not the same as naskh meaning abrogation)

look.title: Four Lines on a Wall
look.text: Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him.
look.cite: Qur'an 112:1-4, Surah Al-Ikhlas, Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: This surah is among the most often written on mosque walls and tiles. Why might a short surah about one God be the one chosen to decorate a building?

check.q: Why did writing become the main visual art of the Muslim world?
choices: Most artists avoided images in religious settings, so writing the Qur'an took that place
Only scribes were allowed in mosques
check.why: Following hadith that warn against images, artists made calligraphy and pattern the arts of the mosque.

check.q: What is Kufic?
check.why: Kufic is the bold angular script of the earliest Qur'ans, including the Blue Qur'an.

check.q: What did Ibn Muqla contribute?
choices: Rules of proportion that led to the rounded naskh script
check.why: Ibn Muqla (d. 940) worked out proportions for a rounder script, the ancestor of the naskh used in printed Qur'ans.

lessons.title: The Mosque as a House of the Book
lessons.mainIdea: A mosque is built around the Qur'an: its niche points toward Mecca, its pulpit carries the sermon, and its walls carry the text.
reading: The Arabic word for mosque, *masjid*, means "place of bowing down." The Qur'an names the first house of worship as the one at Mecca (3:96). Muslim tradition says the Prophet's mosque in Medina was a simple courtyard with a shaded side. From that plan grew later mosques. Damascus, Cordoba, Cairo, Istanbul and Chicago all follow it.

A few parts are found almost everywhere. The *mihrab* is a niche in one wall; it marks the *qibla*, the direction of Mecca, which Surah 2:144 tells believers to face. Beside it stands the *minbar*, a set of steps from which the Friday sermon is given. A tower, the minaret, carries the call to prayer. Inside, there are no chairs and no images, only carpet, light and words.

The words are the Qur'an. Around the mihrab, along the ceiling, over the doors, verses are carved, painted or set in tile. Mosques also became schools. In many, a teacher sat against a pillar and a circle of students learned the Qur'an by heart. Some of the oldest mosques house libraries that hold Qur'an manuscripts a thousand years old.

words.d: the Arabic word for mosque; a place of bowing down in prayer
a niche in a mosque wall that marks the direction of Mecca
the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, which Muslims face in prayer
the stepped pulpit in a mosque from which the Friday sermon is given

look.title: Reading a Room
look.text: Picture a large carpeted hall. One wall has a curved niche, framed in tile with Arabic letters. Next to it, a wooden staircase with a small platform at the top. Along the top of every wall runs a band of writing. There are no benches and no pictures. Shoes are lined up at the door.
look.prompt: Name the parts you can identify and say what each is for. What does the absence of chairs and pictures tell you about how the room is used?

check.q: What does the mihrab mark?
check.why: The mihrab is the niche that shows the qibla, the direction of prayer toward Mecca.

check.q: What is the minbar used for?
choices: Calling the prayer from a tower
check.why: The minbar is the stepped pulpit for the sermon; the call to prayer comes from the minaret.

check.q: What does the word masjid mean?
check.why: Masjid, the root of the English word mosque, means a place of bowing down in prayer.

lessons.title: Grammar for a Sacred Text
lessons.mainIdea: The need to read and recite the Qur'an correctly drove Muslims to write the first full grammar of Arabic.
reading: As Islam spread, most new Muslims did not speak Arabic as a first language. They recited the Qur'an with mistakes. Tradition says that a governor of Iraq heard a reciter misread one vowel and change the meaning of a verse, and ordered scholars to fix the problem. Whether or not the story is exact, the need was real: the text had to be read the same way everywhere.

In the city of Basra in Iraq, scholars began to study Arabic as a system. The greatest of them was Sibawayh (d. c. 796), a Persian by birth. His book, known simply as The Book, describes the grammar of Arabic in detail, using the Qur'an, old poetry and the speech of the Bedouin as its evidence. It is still the foundation of Arabic grammar today.

Grammar fed straight back into tafsir. Recall from the last chapter that 3:7 can be read two ways depending on a pause, and that 5:6 turns on a vowel. A commentator needed grammar to argue for one reading. Dictionaries followed, then studies of rhetoric that asked what made the Qur'an's style unlike other Arabic. The study of the book created the study of the language.

words.d: a scholar of Basra (d. c. 796) whose book is the first full grammar of Arabic
the rules of how a language's words and sentences work

look.title: One Vowel, One Meaning
look.text: In Arabic, short vowels are usually not written. The same three consonants can be read as a noun, a verb or a command depending on the vowels a reader supplies. Now imagine a reciter in a new land, reading a verse aloud in the mosque, and choosing the wrong vowel on the word for God.
look.prompt: Why would a community that recites its scripture aloud feel this problem more sharply than one that only reads silently? What tools would fix it?

check.q: Why did early Muslims need a written grammar of Arabic?
choices: To translate the Qur'an into Latin
So that new Muslims who spoke other languages could recite the Qur'an correctly
check.why: Most new Muslims were not native Arabic speakers, and the text had to be recited the same way everywhere.

check.q: Who wrote the first full grammar of Arabic?
check.why: Sibawayh (d. c. 796) of Basra wrote The Book, still the foundation of Arabic grammar.

check.q: How did grammar help commentators?
choices: It told them which surahs were Meccan
It replaced the need for tafsir
It let them argue for one reading of a verse over another
check.why: Questions such as where to pause in 3:7 or how to vowel a word in 5:6 are settled with grammar.

lessons.title: Stars, Calendars and the House of Wisdom
lessons.mainIdea: Practical needs set by the Qur'an, the lunar calendar and the direction of prayer, helped drive Muslim work in astronomy and mathematics.
reading: The Qur'an sets a lunar calendar. Surah 2:189 speaks of the new moons as markers of time for people and for the pilgrimage. Surah 2:185 ties fasting to the month of Ramadan. A month begins when the new crescent is seen. To know when Ramadan starts, Muslims needed to predict the moon. The five daily prayers are timed by the sun. Every mosque must face Mecca.

These needs made astronomy a religious science. Muslim astronomers built observatories and refined star tables. They worked out how to find the qibla from any city on earth, a hard problem in geometry. The astrolabe is an instrument for measuring the sky. It was improved for prayer times and became a standard tool across the Muslim world.

In the early 800s, in Baghdad, the caliph al-Ma'mun supported a circle of translators and scholars often called the House of Wisdom. Greek, Persian and Indian works on mathematics, medicine and the stars were translated into Arabic. Al-Khwarizmi, who worked there around 820, wrote the book that gave us the word algebra. The word algorithm comes from his name.

Historians debate how much of this science flowed from the Qur'an itself. Some of it came from the wealth and curiosity of a huge new empire. Both were at work. What is clear is this. The Qur'an's calendar and qibla gave astronomers a daily reason to look up. And the Arabic language, spread by the Qur'an, let a scholar in Spain read a scholar in Persia.

words.d: a calendar based on the moon's cycle; the Islamic year has twelve lunar months
a circle of scholars and translators in Baghdad in the early 800s, supported by the caliph al-Ma'mun
an instrument for measuring the positions of the sun and stars; used to find prayer times

look.title: The New Moons
look.text: The Qur'an says people ask about the new moons, and answers that they are fixed times for people and for the pilgrimage.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:189, Surah Al-Baqarah, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: What practical problems does a moon-based calendar create for a community spread across many countries, and what kinds of knowledge would solve them?

check.q: Why did Muslim scholars need to predict the moon?
choices: Because months such as Ramadan begin with the new crescent
check.why: The Islamic calendar is lunar, and fasting and pilgrimage are tied to particular months.

check.q: What was the House of Wisdom?
choices: A circle of scholars and translators in Baghdad in the early 800s
check.why: The caliph al-Ma'mun supported translators and scholars in Baghdad; al-Khwarizmi worked in that circle.

check.q: Which word comes from the name of the scholar al-Khwarizmi?
check.why: Algorithm comes from al-Khwarizmi's name; algebra comes from the title of his book.

lessons.title: Madrasa: Schools of the Book
lessons.mainIdea: The madrasa, a school for Qur'an, hadith and law, spread across the Muslim world and trained the scholars who interpreted the text.
reading: A *madrasa* is simply a school. In the Muslim world the word came to mean a school for religious learning: Qur'an, hadith, grammar and law. Early teaching happened in mosques. By the 800s and 900s, wealthy patrons were founding buildings with classrooms, a library and rooms where students could live. The teacher had a salary; the students had a place to sleep.

Some of these schools still exist. Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco, was founded in 859 by a woman, Fatima al-Fihri, according to tradition. Al-Azhar in Cairo opened around 970 and remains a leading center of Sunni learning. The Nizamiyya in Baghdad, founded in 1065, set a model that was copied across the Middle East. Al-Ghazali, whom you met in the last chapter, taught there.

Madrasas trained the ulama. A student memorized the Qur'an, then learned grammar, then hadith, then the law of one school. When finished, a teacher gave the student a license to teach a particular book. This chain of teacher and student, like the chain of a hadith, was written down and kept. Madrasas spread to India, West Africa and Southeast Asia and still exist alongside modern schools.

words.d: a school, especially one for Qur'an, hadith, grammar and Islamic law
a mosque and school in Cairo, opened around 970, a leading center of Sunni learning

look.title: Old Schools, Still Teaching
look.cite: Founding dates as commonly given in reference works; early dates are approximate
look.prompt: What do the first three schools have in common with the last two? What was taught in each, and who paid for it?

check.q: What did a madrasa teach?
check.why: A madrasa was a school for religious learning; the Qur'an came first, then grammar, hadith and law.

check.q: Which school does tradition say was founded by Fatima al-Fihri in 859?
check.why: Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco, is traditionally dated to 859 and credited to Fatima al-Fihri.

check.q: What did a student receive on finishing a book with a teacher?
choices: A place in the Six Books
A copy of the Blue Qur'an
A license to teach that book
check.why: The license recorded the chain of teacher and student, much as an isnad records a hadith's chain.

lessons.title: One Book, Many Tongues
lessons.mainIdea: From Persia to Indonesia, Muslims kept the Qur'an in Arabic but explained and translated it in their own languages.
reading: The Arabic Qur'an moved into worlds that spoke other languages. Muslim scholars generally held that a translation is not the Qur'an itself. It is an explanation of it. That view allowed translation while keeping recitation in Arabic. Tradition says the first full Persian rendering was made in the 900s. Al-Tabari's tafsir was translated then for a ruler in Central Asia.

Persian became the second great language of Islam. Poets such as Rumi (d. 1273) wove Qur'an verses into their verse. Ottoman Turks carried the book to the Balkans and wrote it in their own script based on Arabic. In South Asia, Urdu grew up as a language written in Arabic letters, and Urdu commentaries are read by millions today.

On the East African coast, Swahili Muslims wrote poems about the prophets in Arabic script. In Southeast Asia, Malay was written in a script called Jawi. The Qur'an reached the islands of Indonesia, today the country with the most Muslims in the world. In each place, the sound stayed Arabic and the explanation took the local tongue.

words.d: a rendering of a text into another language; most Muslim scholars hold that a translation of the Qur'an explains it but is not the Qur'an itself
a script based on Arabic letters used to write Malay

look.title: Where Muslims Live Today
look.cite: Rounded from widely cited demographic estimates (Pew Research Center, c. 2020)
look.prompt: None of these six countries speaks Arabic as its main language. What does that tell you about how the Qur'an is read and heard by most Muslims?

check.q: How do most Muslim scholars describe a translation of the Qur'an?
choices: As an explanation of the Qur'an, not the Qur'an itself
check.why: Because the Qur'an is held to be Arabic, a translation is treated as commentary; recitation stays in Arabic.

check.q: Which country has the largest number of Muslims?
check.why: Indonesia, in Southeast Asia, has more Muslims than any other country by common estimates.

check.q: What is Jawi?
choices: A script based on Arabic letters used for Malay
check.why: Jawi is the Arabic-based script in which Malay was written.

lessons.title: From Latin to English
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an was first translated into Latin in 1143 and into English from Arabic in 1734, at first by outsiders who wanted to argue with it.
reading: The first translation of the Qur'an into a European language was made in 1143. Peter the Venerable, abbot of the great monastery of Cluny in France, paid an Englishman named Robert of Ketton to render it into Latin. Peter wanted Christians to know what Muslims believed so they could argue against it. His purpose was not neutral, but his project put the text in European hands. That Latin version was printed in 1543.

English came later. In 1649 Alexander Ross published an English Qur'an, but he translated from a French version, not from Arabic. The first English translation made directly from Arabic was by George Sale in 1734. Sale, a lawyer, added a long introduction and notes drawn from Muslim commentators. His book was read for two centuries. Thomas Jefferson bought a copy in 1765.

In the 1800s came J. M. Rodwell (1861), a clergyman who rearranged the surahs into what he thought was their historical order, and E. H. Palmer (1880), a Cambridge scholar who aimed for plain speech. Each translator had a purpose. Reading them side by side shows how much a translator's choices shape what a reader hears.

words.d: an English scholar who made the first Latin translation of the Qur'an in 1143
an English lawyer whose 1734 translation was the first English Qur'an made from Arabic

look.title: Two Translators, Two Purposes
look.text: Peter the Venerable (1143): wanted Christians to read the Qur'an so they could argue against Islam. George Sale (1734): wrote that a translator should let readers judge the book for themselves, and filled his notes with Muslim commentators. Both made the Qur'an available to people who could not read Arabic.
look.prompt: Can a translation made to argue against a book still be useful for studying it? What would you check in each translation before trusting it?

check.q: Who paid for the first Latin translation of the Qur'an?
choices: Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny
check.why: Peter the Venerable commissioned Robert of Ketton's Latin version in 1143.

check.q: What was different about George Sale's 1734 translation?
choices: It was the first English version made directly from Arabic
check.why: Ross (1649) worked from French; Sale worked from Arabic and added notes from Muslim commentators.

check.q: What did J. M. Rodwell do that other translators did not?
choices: He rearranged the surahs into what he thought was their historical order
He worked at the House of Wisdom
He refused to name the surahs
check.why: Rodwell's 1861 translation reorders the surahs; most translations keep the traditional order.

lessons.title: Muslim Translators in English
lessons.mainIdea: In the twentieth century Muslims began translating the Qur'an into English themselves, and Pickthall (1930) and Yusuf Ali (1934) became the most read.
reading: Until the 1900s, nearly every English Qur'an was made by a non-Muslim. That changed with Marmaduke Pickthall. He was an English novelist who became a Muslim in 1917. He worked in India under the patronage of the ruler of Hyderabad. In 1930 he published The Meaning of the Glorious Koran. Note the title. He called it the meaning, not the Qur'an. That follows the scholars' view that a translation is an explanation.

Pickthall's English is deliberately old-fashioned, with "thee" and "thou" and "hath." He wanted it to sound like the King James Bible his readers knew. His translation is now in the public domain in the United States. That is why this course quotes it. Four years later, Abdullah Yusuf Ali, an Indian civil servant, published a translation with thousands of notes. It became the most widely printed English Qur'an of the century.

Since then, dozens of English translations have appeared. Some are by Muslims of many backgrounds, some by scholars who are not Muslim. Some aim for modern plain English. Some try to catch the sound of the Arabic. Some add long commentary. Muslim readers in Chicago often keep two or three on the shelf and compare them, much as al-Tabari compared reports.

words.d: Marmaduke Pickthall, English Muslim whose 1930 translation is this course's text
Abdullah Yusuf Ali, whose 1934 translation with notes became the most printed English Qur'an of the century
works no longer under copyright, which anyone may quote and reprint

look.title: Landmark Translations
look.cite: Publication dates as given on the title pages and in standard bibliographies
look.prompt: How long was the gap between the first Latin and the first English-from-Arabic version? What changed in 1930?

check.q: Why did Pickthall call his book The Meaning of the Glorious Koran?
choices: Because he translated only part of it
Because scholars hold that a translation is an explanation, not the Qur'an itself
Because the publisher chose the title
Because he did not know Arabic
check.why: Pickthall followed the traditional view that only the Arabic is the Qur'an; a translation gives its meaning.

check.q: Why does this course quote Pickthall rather than Yusuf Ali?
choices: Pickthall's translation is in the public domain; Yusuf Ali's is not
check.why: Pickthall's 1930 text may be quoted freely; later translations are under copyright and are only described.

check.q: What was new about the 1930s translations?
choices: They were the first in Latin
They were the first made from French
They were made by the House of Wisdom
They were made by Muslims for English readers
check.why: Pickthall and Yusuf Ali were the first widely read English translations by Muslims.

lessons.title: Muslims in Chains
lessons.mainIdea: Tens of thousands of enslaved Africans brought to America were Muslims, and a few left writings that show the Qur'an lived in their memory.
reading: The Qur'an came to America before the United States existed. Historians estimate that a meaningful share of the Africans enslaved and brought to North America came from Muslim regions of West Africa, though the numbers are uncertain. Many were literate in Arabic. Most left no record. A few did, and their writings are among the oldest Muslim documents in the country.

Ayuba Suleiman Diallo, also called Job ben Solomon, was enslaved in Maryland in the 1730s. Taken to England, he is said to have written out the Qur'an from memory. Bilali Muhammad, enslaved on Sapelo Island, Georgia, wrote a short Arabic manuscript on Islamic law and practice in the early 1800s. It is kept at the University of Georgia. And Omar ibn Said, whom you met at the start of this chapter, wrote his life in North Carolina in 1831.

These writings raise hard questions. Omar's story praises his owners and mentions attending church. Some scholars read this as real change; others see a careful man writing for readers who held power over him. His manuscript begins with a surah about God's kingdom. Both readings are possible, and the debate itself shows how much a text depends on who reads it and why.

words.d: a West African Muslim scholar enslaved in North Carolina who wrote his life story in Arabic in 1831
a document written by hand

look.title: The Kingdom
look.text: Surah 67 opens by blessing the One in whose hand is all dominion, who has power over all things, who created death and life to test which of you is best in conduct. Omar ibn Said wrote this surah out from memory at the start of his life story.
look.cite: Qur'an 67:1-2, Surah Al-Mulk, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930); Omar ibn Said, The Life of Omar ibn Said (1831), Library of Congress
look.prompt: Some scholars read Omar's choice of this surah as a quiet statement about who truly rules. What in the surah's opening supports that reading? What other reasons might he have had?

check.q: When did the Qur'an first reach what is now the United States?
choices: In the memory of enslaved West African Muslims, before the nation was founded
check.why: Muslims from West Africa were among the enslaved people brought to the colonies; a few left Arabic writings.

check.q: What did Bilali Muhammad write?
choices: A translation of the Qur'an into English
A short Arabic manuscript on Islamic law and practice
check.why: Bilali Muhammad of Sapelo Island, Georgia, wrote an Arabic manuscript on law and practice, kept at the University of Georgia.

check.q: Why do scholars disagree about Omar ibn Said's life story?
choices: Because it is written in Latin
Because it praises his owners and mentions church, yet opens with a surah about God's kingdom
Because he never learned to write
check.why: The text can be read as real change or as careful writing for powerful readers; the opening surah supports the second reading.

lessons.title: Jefferson's Qur'an and the 1893 Parliament
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an entered American public life through a founder's library, a world's fair in Chicago, and later through the oath of a congressman.
reading: In 1765, a young lawyer in Virginia named Thomas Jefferson bought George Sale's English Qur'an. He was studying law and wanted to know other systems. His copy is still in the Library of Congress. Historians note that Jefferson's interest was legal and comparative. He did not become a Muslim, and his views on Islam were mixed.

In 1893, Chicago hosted the World's Columbian Exposition. Beside it met the World's Parliament of Religions, the first large gathering of the world's faiths. Among the speakers was Mohammed Alexander Russell Webb. He was an American journalist and former diplomat who had become a Muslim. He spoke about Islam to an audience that had mostly never met a Muslim. The Parliament is remembered today as a starting point for interfaith conversation in the United States.

In 2007, Keith Ellison of Minnesota became the first Muslim elected to Congress. For his ceremonial oath he placed his hand on Jefferson's copy of the Qur'an. The Library of Congress lent it for the day. The moment tied together three things. The founder's library, the enslaved scholars who came before, and the Muslim citizens of the present.

words.d: a gathering of the world's faiths held in Chicago in 1893
an American journalist who became a Muslim and spoke about Islam at the 1893 Parliament

look.title: A Book on a Shelf, a Book in a Hand
look.text: Scene one, 1765: a law student in Virginia buys a two-volume English Qur'an to learn how other people write laws. Scene two, 2007: a newly elected congressman lays his hand on those same volumes for his ceremonial oath. Same book, same pages, 242 years apart.
look.prompt: What did the book mean to each man? What does it tell you that a copy bought for study became a symbol of belonging?

check.q: Why did Thomas Jefferson buy a Qur'an in 1765?
choices: He was studying law and wanted to know other systems
It was required at William and Mary
check.why: Jefferson bought Sale's translation as a law student; historians describe his interest as comparative.

check.q: Where was the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions held?
check.why: The Parliament met in Chicago beside the World's Columbian Exposition.

check.q: Who took a ceremonial oath on Jefferson's Qur'an in 2007?
check.why: Keith Ellison, the first Muslim elected to Congress, borrowed Jefferson's copy from the Library of Congress.

lessons.title: The Qur'an in Chicago Today
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's Muslim community is one of the largest and most varied in the country, and the Qur'an is read there in every way this course has described.
reading: The Chicago area today has one of the largest Muslim communities in the United States. Estimates vary widely, but they run to several hundred thousand people. They come from South Asia, the Arab world, Africa, Bosnia, Turkey and Southeast Asia. Many are African American families whose Muslim roots in the city go back a century. Dozens of mosques serve them. They range from the large Mosque Foundation in suburban Bridgeview to storefront prayer rooms on Devon Avenue.

The city has its own chapter in American Muslim history. The Nation of Islam, founded in Detroit in 1930, made its headquarters in Chicago. Its teachings differed from those of most Muslims worldwide. In 1975, under Warith Deen Mohammed, most of its members moved toward mainstream Sunni Islam, one of the largest religious shifts in American history. Their descendants read the Qur'an in Chicago mosques today.

Everything in this unit can be seen in the city. Children in weekend schools memorize surahs in Arabic. Study circles read Ibn Kathir in English. Sunni and Shia mosques stand a few miles apart. Sufi groups gather for remembrance. Calligraphy hangs in homes. And at interfaith events, heirs of the 1893 Parliament, Muslims read the Qur'an aloud beside Jews reading the Torah and Christians reading the Gospels, each explaining their book to the others.

words.d: an American movement founded in 1930 and based in Chicago; most of its members moved toward Sunni Islam in 1975
involving people of different religions meeting, talking and learning about one another's traditions

look.title: One Weekend in the City
look.text: Saturday morning, a weekend school in a suburb: forty children recite Surah Al-Fatiha together in Arabic. Saturday evening, a living room on the North Side: six adults read a page of Ibn Kathir in English and argue about it. Sunday afternoon, a church hall downtown: a rabbi, an imam and a pastor each read a passage about Ibrahim (Abraham) to a mixed audience.
look.prompt: Match each scene to a practice from this unit: recitation, tafsir, interfaith reading. Which of the three would have surprised a scholar in Baghdad in the year 900, and which would he have recognized at once?

check.q: Which statement about Chicago's Muslim community is accurate?
choices: It is one of the largest and most varied in the United States
It is made up only of recent immigrants
It follows a single school of law
check.why: Chicago's Muslims number in the hundreds of thousands and come from many backgrounds, including families with a century of roots in the city.

check.q: What happened to the Nation of Islam in 1975?
choices: Most of its members moved toward mainstream Sunni Islam under Warith Deen Mohammed
It published a translation of the Qur'an
check.why: Under Warith Deen Mohammed, most members shifted toward Sunni Islam, one of the largest religious changes in American history.

check.q: Which practice from this unit would a scholar of Baghdad in 900 have recognized at once?
choices: Reading the Qur'an on a phone
An interfaith panel in a church hall
Children reciting a surah in Arabic from memory
An English translation by a Muslim
check.why: Memorized recitation of the Arabic text is the oldest practice; translation into English and modern interfaith panels are recent.

review.q: Which languages adopted the Arabic alphabet as Islam spread?
choices: Persian, Ottoman Turkish, Urdu, Swahili and Malay
review.why: The Qur'an's alphabet traveled with the book and was used to write many languages of Muslim peoples.

review.q: Why is calligraphy the main religious art of the Muslim world?
choices: Most artists avoided images in religious settings, so writing the Qur'an took that place
Paint was forbidden by the caliphs
review.why: Following hadith that warn against images, artists turned to writing the Qur'an beautifully and to geometric pattern.

review.q: What does the mihrab in a mosque show?
review.why: The mihrab marks the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca.

review.q: What religious needs helped drive Muslim astronomy?
choices: The lunar calendar, prayer times and finding the direction of Mecca
review.why: Ramadan and the pilgrimage depend on the moon, prayer on the sun, and every mosque must face Mecca.

choices: A tower for the call to prayer
A school for Qur'an, hadith, grammar and law
review.why: Madrasas such as al-Azhar and the Nizamiyya trained the ulama.

review.q: Who made the first English translation of the Qur'an directly from Arabic?
review.why: Sale worked from Arabic; Ketton wrote Latin; Ross translated from French; Pickthall came two centuries later.

review.q: What is special about Omar ibn Said's 1831 manuscript?
choices: It is the first Qur'an printed in America
It is the Arabic life story of an enslaved Muslim scholar, opening with Surah 67
It is a translation by Thomas Jefferson
It was read at the 1893 Parliament
review.why: Omar ibn Said, enslaved in North Carolina, wrote his life in Arabic and began with Surah Al-Mulk; the Library of Congress holds it.

review.q: What was the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions?
choices: A meeting of the four schools of law
A gathering of the world's faiths in Chicago, where Islam was presented to Americans
The founding of the Nation of Islam
review.why: The Parliament met in Chicago in 1893; Mohammed Alexander Russell Webb spoke there about Islam.
